learn.hook: One mountain range, one ocean, and around a quarter of humanity in between. South Asia is a region of shared geography but very different political systems.
points: South Asia usually includes Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka. Afghanistan and Myanmar are often included in discussions of the region.
Geography gives the region a natural unity: the Himalayas in the north, the Indian Ocean, the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal to the south, west and east.

Politically the region is very diverse: India and Sri Lanka have kept democratic systems since independence, Pakistan and Bangladesh have alternated between civilian and military rule, Nepal moved from monarchy to a republic, and Bhutan is a constitutional monarchy.

Map work: Islamabad (Pakistan), Dhaka (Bangladesh), Kathmandu (Nepal), Thimphu (Bhutan), Malé (the Maldives), New Delhi (India), Kabul (Afghanistan). Sri Lanka's official capital is Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte, with Colombo as its commercial capital.

example.q: A map question asks you to mark the capitals of three Himalayan neighbours of India. Name them.
steps: Pakistan: Islamabad (its north lies in the Himalaya-Karakoram region).

learn.reallife: The monsoon that waters Indian farms also feeds rivers flowing through Nepal, Bhutan and Bangladesh. Shared rivers and weather tie the region together.

games.title: Democratic all along, or mixed record?
buckets: Alternated between democracy and non-democratic rule

quiz.q: Which of these is the capital of Bhutan?
quiz.explain: Thimphu is Bhutan's capital; Kathmandu is Nepal's.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up Bhutan and Nepal

quiz.q: Which country is NOT usually counted in the core list of South Asian countries?
quiz.explain: Indonesia is in Southeast Asia and belongs to ASEAN.
quiz.mistake: Confuses South Asia with Southeast Asia

quiz.q: Which two countries are often included in discussions of South Asia besides the seven core countries?
quiz.explain: Afghanistan and Myanmar are frequently discussed as part of the region.
quiz.mistake: Picks distant countries

quiz.q: The capital of the Maldives is:
quiz.explain: Malé is the capital of the island nation of the Maldives.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with Sri Lanka's commercial capital

quiz.q: Which natural feature forms South Asia's northern boundary?
quiz.explain: The Himalayas lie to the north; seas and the ocean lie to the south.
quiz.mistake: Swaps north and south

quiz.q: Which statement about political systems in South Asia is correct?
options: All countries have always been monarchies
They are diverse: democracies, monarchies and periods of military rule
All countries have always been military dictatorships
All have the same constitution as India
quiz.explain: The region has a wide variety of political systems.
quiz.mistake: Assumes a single system for the whole region

quiz.q: Assertion (A): South Asia has a distinctive geographic unity. Reason (R): It is bounded by the Himalayas in the north and by seas and the Indian Ocean in the south.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; the natural boundaries give the region its unity.
quiz.mistake: Fails to link physical boundaries with regional unity

quiz.q: Assertion (A): India and Sri Lanka have remained democracies since independence. Reason (R): Bhutan is a republic with no king.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true. R is false: Bhutan is a constitutional monarchy.
quiz.mistake: Confuses Bhutan's system with Nepal's

teach.ask: Gappu flaps: 'Which countries are in South Asia? And are they all run the same way?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Seven core countries, tied by the Himalayas and the ocean, but each with very different politics!
teach.nudge: Can you name the countries and tell me if they all have the same kind of government?

topics.title: The military and democracy in Pakistan

learn.hook: Pakistan's history reads like a relay race between generals and elected leaders, with the baton changing hands again and again.
points: After Pakistan framed its first constitution, General Ayub Khan took over in 1958 and soon got himself elected. Popular dissatisfaction forced him out, and General Yahya Khan took over in 1969.

After the 1971 war, an elected government under Zulfikar Ali Bhutto ruled from 1971 to 1977. General Zia-ul-Haq removed it in 1977. A pro-democracy movement led to an elected government under Benazir Bhutto in 1988.

Elected governments of Benazir Bhutto and Nawaz Sharif followed. In 1999 the army under General Pervez Musharraf took over again. Since 2008 elected civilian governments have ruled, but the army keeps great influence.

Reasons for weak democracy: the social dominance of the military, the clergy and the landowning aristocracy; conflict with India strengthening pro-military groups; and support for military rule from the USA and others during the Cold War.

example.q: Order these leaders in Pakistan's history: Zia-ul-Haq, Ayub Khan, Pervez Musharraf, Benazir Bhutto.
example.answer: Ayub Khan → Zia-ul-Haq → Benazir Bhutto → Pervez Musharraf

learn.reallife: When Indian and Pakistani teams meet at cricket, commentators often note how differently the two countries' institutions evolved after 1947, even though both started from the same colonial system.

quiz.q: Who took over Pakistan's administration in 1958?
quiz.explain: Ayub Khan's takeover in 1958 began military rule.
quiz.mistake: Picks a later military ruler

quiz.q: Which general removed Zulfikar Ali Bhutto's government in 1977?
quiz.explain: General Zia-ul-Haq took over in 1977.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the order of military rulers

quiz.q: In 1988, a democratically elected government came to power in Pakistan under:
quiz.explain: Benazir Bhutto led the government elected in 1988.
quiz.mistake: Picks Nawaz Sharif, who came later

quiz.q: The army took over in Pakistan again in 1999 under:
quiz.explain: Musharraf removed the elected government in 1999.
quiz.mistake: Picks an earlier military ruler

quiz.q: Which is a reason for the failure of democracy to take firm root in Pakistan?
options: Social dominance of the military, clergy and landowning aristocracy
A strong tradition of independent courts and free press from the start
Too many free and fair elections
quiz.explain: These groups dominated society and weakened democratic institutions.
quiz.mistake: Overlooks the power of the army and elites

quiz.q: How did the Cold War affect democracy in Pakistan?
options: The USA and others backed military rulers for their own strategic interests
The USA forced Pakistan to remain a monarchy
The Cold War had no link with Pakistan
quiz.explain: Outside powers tolerated or supported military regimes that served their interests.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the role of external support

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Pro-military groups in Pakistan became stronger over time. Reason (R): Pakistan's conflicts with India made the army's role seem more important.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; tension with India strengthened arguments for military influence.
quiz.mistake: Fails to link external conflict with internal military power

quiz.q: Case: A Pakistani elected government holds office, but major decisions on defence and foreign policy are shaped by army generals. Which feature of Pakistan's politics does this show?
options: Continued army influence over elected governments
quiz.explain: Even under civilian rule, the army keeps strong influence.
quiz.mistake: Assumes elections alone remove military influence

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does Pakistan keep switching between generals and elected leaders?'
teach.praise: Hoot! The army, clergy and landlords are powerful, tensions with India help the army, and the Cold War backing hurt democracy too!
teach.nudge: You named the generals. But WHY was democracy weak there?

learn.hook: In 1971 a people won a war to protect their language and their vote. Building a stable democracy afterwards proved just as hard as winning freedom.
points: From 1947 to 1971, Bangladesh was East Pakistan. Its people resented domination by West Pakistan and the imposition of Urdu. Sheikh Mujibur Rahman of the Awami League led the struggle for autonomy.

In the 1970 elections, the Awami League won almost all the seats in East Pakistan (160 of 162), giving it a majority in the proposed Constituent Assembly. The West Pakistan leadership refused to accept this, and the army under General Yahya Khan cracked down and arrested Sheikh Mujib.
Millions fled to India as refugees. India supported the freedom struggle, and after war in December 1971, Bangladesh became independent.

Bangladesh's constitution declared it secular, democratic and socialist. In 1975 Sheikh Mujib changed it to a presidential system and abolished all parties except the Awami League; he was assassinated that year in a military uprising.

Military-led rule followed (Ziaur Rahman, then H.M. Ershad). A mass protest movement forced Ershad to step down in 1990, and since 1991 Bangladesh has had a representative democracy with multi-party elections.

example.q: Order: Ershad steps down; Bangladesh becomes independent; Awami League wins 1970 elections; Sheikh Mujib assassinated.
steps: 1970: Awami League sweeps elections in East Pakistan.
1990: Ershad steps down after mass protests.

learn.reallife: Bangladesh's garment factories now dress the world, and India and Bangladesh share rail, road and power links. The two countries share a history from 1971.

items.text: Before 1971, Bangladesh was known as East ___.
Sheikh Mujibur Rahman led the ___ League.
After Sheikh Mujib, military-led governments included those of Ziaur Rahman and H.M. ___.
Since ___, Bangladesh has had multi-party elections.

quiz.q: Before 1971, Bangladesh was known as:
quiz.explain: It was the eastern wing of Pakistan from 1947 to 1971.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with the Indian state of West Bengal

quiz.q: Who led the Awami League in the struggle for Bangladesh?
quiz.explain: Sheikh Mujib led the Awami League and the freedom movement.
quiz.mistake: Picks a West Pakistan leader

quiz.q: In the 1970 elections, the Awami League:
options: Won almost all seats in East Pakistan
quiz.explain: Its sweep gave it a majority in the proposed Constituent Assembly.
quiz.mistake: Underestimates the Awami League's victory

quiz.q: Which change did Sheikh Mujib make to the constitution in 1975?
options: He introduced a presidential system and abolished all parties except the Awami League
quiz.explain: These changes concentrated power before his assassination later in 1975.
quiz.mistake: Assumes 1975 marked democratic expansion

quiz.q: Bangladesh has had representative democracy based on multi-party elections since:
quiz.explain: After Ershad stepped down in 1990, elections in 1991 restored democracy.
quiz.mistake: Confuses independence with the restoration of democracy

quiz.q: India's role in 1971 was to:
options: Support the freedom struggle of the people of East Pakistan
quiz.explain: India backed the struggle, and the December 1971 war led to Bangladesh's independence.
quiz.mistake: Thinks India annexed the region

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The people of East Pakistan resented West Pakistan's domination. Reason (R): Urdu was imposed on them, and their elected majority was not honoured.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; R explains the resentment.
quiz.mistake: Overlooks language and denial of electoral victory

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Bangladesh has never had military-led rule. Reason (R): The constitution of Bangladesh originally declared it secular, democratic and socialist.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: Ziaur Rahman and Ershad led military-backed rule. R is true.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the military period of 1975-1990

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How was Bangladesh born, and has it always been a democracy?'
teach.praise: Brilliant! East Pakistan became Bangladesh in 1971 under Sheikh Mujib, went through military rule, and has had multi-party democracy since 1991!
teach.nudge: You told me how it was born. What happened to democracy after 1975?

learn.hook: In 2008 a country with one of the world's oldest ruling dynasties voted to abolish its monarchy. Nepal's path from king to republic took decades of protest.
points: Nepal was a Hindu kingdom in the past, and then a constitutional monarchy for many years in the modern period.
A strong pro-democracy movement in 1990 forced the king to accept a new democratic constitution. Democratic governments that followed were short-lived and troubled.
In the 1990s the Maoists, who opposed the monarchy and the ruling elite, built an armed insurgency in many parts of Nepal. In 2002 the king abolished the parliament and dismissed the government.
In April 2006 massive, country-wide pro-democracy protests by the Seven-Party Alliance (SPA), the Maoists and social activists forced the king to restore the House of Representatives.
In 2008 Nepal abolished the monarchy and became a democratic republic. A new Constitution was adopted in 2015.

example.q: Order these milestones in Nepal: monarchy abolished; king accepts democratic constitution after protests; new Constitution adopted; king restores parliament after mass protests.
steps: 2006: king restores the House of Representatives.

learn.reallife: India and Nepal share an open border; millions of Nepali citizens work in India and many have served in the Indian Army's Gorkha regiments, so Nepal's political changes are followed closely in India.

games.title: True or false?
items: The Maoists supported the absolute power of the king.
They opposed the monarchy and the ruling elite.
Nepal's new Constitution was adopted in 2015.
It came after the long constitution-making process.
The 2006 protests were led by the army.
They were led by the Seven-Party Alliance, the Maoists and social activists.
In 1990 the king accepted a new democratic constitution.
A strong pro-democracy movement forced this.

quiz.q: Nepal abolished its monarchy and became a democratic republic in:
quiz.explain: The monarchy ended in 2008; the new Constitution came in 2015.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the end of monarchy with the new Constitution

quiz.q: Which group led an armed insurgency against the monarchy in Nepal from the 1990s?
quiz.explain: The Maoists fought against the monarchy and the ruling elite.
quiz.mistake: Picks a group from another South Asian country

quiz.q: The April 2006 pro-democracy movement in Nepal forced the king to:
quiz.explain: The king restored the parliament he had dissolved.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the 2006 movement immediately abolished the monarchy

quiz.q: Nepal's new Constitution was adopted in:
quiz.explain: After the monarchy was abolished, a new Constitution came in 2015.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the Constitution came the same year as the republic

quiz.q: What did the 1990 pro-democracy movement in Nepal achieve?
options: The king accepted a new democratic constitution
quiz.explain: The 1990 movement brought a democratic constitution while the monarchy continued.
quiz.mistake: Confuses 1990 with 2008

quiz.q: Who were part of the 2006 movement for democracy in Nepal?
options: The Seven-Party Alliance, the Maoists and social activists
quiz.explain: A broad coalition joined the protests.
quiz.mistake: Thinks one group alone led the movement

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Nepal is now a democratic republic. Reason (R): Its monarchy was abolished in 2008.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; the abolition of the monarchy made Nepal a republic.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect abolition of monarchy with republic status

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Democracy in Nepal was fully stable after 1990. Reason (R): The Maoist insurgency spread in many parts of Nepal in the 1990s.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: the 1990s were turbulent. R is true.
quiz.mistake: Assumes one constitution solved all problems

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Nepal had a king? What happened to him, and when?'
teach.praise: Wow! A king, protests in 1990 and 2006, the Maoist insurgency, and finally a republic in 2008 with a Constitution in 2015!
teach.nudge: When exactly did Nepal stop having a king? And who pushed for it?

topics.title: Ethnic conflict and democracy in Sri Lanka

learn.hook: Sri Lanka has kept holding elections since 1948, yet for over two decades it also fought one of Asia's longest civil wars.
points: Sri Lanka has remained a democracy since independence in 1948, but faced a serious ethnic conflict. Sinhala nationalists believed Sri Lanka should belong to the Sinhala majority and resisted concessions to the Tamil minority.

Neglect of Tamil concerns led to militant Tamil nationalism. From 1983 the LTTE (Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam) fought an armed struggle against the army, demanding 'Tamil Eelam', a separate country for Sri Lankan Tamils.

In 1987 India signed an accord with Sri Lanka and sent the Indian Peace Keeping Force (IPKF) to help stabilise the situation. The IPKF got into fighting with the LTTE, and the move was unpopular among many Sri Lankans and Tamils in India. The IPKF was withdrawn without achieving its aim.
The conflict ended in 2009 when the LTTE was defeated by the Sri Lankan army.

Despite the conflict, Sri Lanka recorded considerable economic growth and high levels of human development. It was one of the first developing countries to control population growth and the first in the region to liberalise its economy.

example.q: Explain why the LTTE demanded Tamil Eelam.
steps: Sinhala majority nationalism dominated politics after 1948.
Tamil concerns were neglected, causing alienation.
Militant Tamil groups, led by the LTTE from 1983, demanded a separate country, Tamil Eelam.
example.answer: Because of Sinhala majoritarianism and neglect of Tamil concerns

learn.reallife: Tamil Nadu and northern Sri Lanka are separated only by the narrow Palk Strait, which is why events in Sri Lanka have always drawn strong interest in Indian politics.

games.title: Match the term
pairs: Separate country demanded by the LTTE

quiz.q: What does LTTE stand for?
quiz.explain: The LTTE fought for Tamil Eelam.
quiz.mistake: Expands the acronym wrongly

quiz.q: India sent the Indian Peace Keeping Force (IPKF) to Sri Lanka in:
quiz.explain: India signed an accord and sent the IPKF in 1987.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with the start of the LTTE war (1983) or its end (2009)

quiz.q: The civil war in Sri Lanka ended in 2009 when:
options: The LTTE was defeated by the Sri Lankan army
The UN took over Sri Lanka
quiz.explain: The army defeated the LTTE in 2009.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the conflict ended in a separate state

quiz.q: The root of the ethnic conflict in Sri Lanka was:
options: Sinhala majoritarianism and neglect of the Tamil minority
Conflict between Buddhists and Christians over the capital
quiz.explain: Majority domination alienated Tamils.
quiz.mistake: Looks for an external cause

quiz.q: Which statement about Sri Lanka's development is correct?
options: It has the highest population growth in South Asia
It achieved high levels of human development despite the conflict
quiz.explain: It controlled population growth early and was the first in the region to liberalise.
quiz.mistake: Assumes conflict prevented all development

quiz.q: Why was the IPKF intervention unpopular?
options: It was sent to support the LTTE's demand
The IPKF ended up fighting the LTTE and many Sri Lankans saw it as interference
quiz.explain: It became entangled in fighting and was widely criticised.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the IPKF supported the LTTE

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Sri Lanka has retained a democratic political system since independence. Reason (R): Sri Lanka faced a long ethnic conflict.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true, but the conflict does not explain why democracy survived.
quiz.mistake: Treats two facts as cause and effect

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Sri Lanka was the first country in South Asia to liberalise its economy. Reason (R): The LTTE won the civil war and created Tamil Eelam.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true. R is false: the LTTE was defeated in 2009.
quiz.mistake: Mistakes the outcome of the war

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Sri Lanka is a democracy, so why was there a war there?'
teach.praise: Oh! Sinhala majoritarianism hurt the Tamils, the LTTE fought for Tamil Eelam, India sent the IPKF in 1987, and the war ended in 2009.
teach.nudge: Good start. What did the LTTE want, and how did India get involved?

learn.hook: Two countries born on the same night in 1947 have fought several wars, share rivers, and in 1998 both declared themselves nuclear powers.
points: Kashmir has been the core issue between India and Pakistan since Partition. They fought wars in 1947-48 and 1965. In 1971 war broke out over East Pakistan, leading to Bangladesh. In 1999 they fought the Kargil conflict.
Other disputes include control of the Siachen glacier and the boundary line in Sir Creek, a strip of water in the Rann of Kutch.
River waters: the Indus Waters Treaty was signed in 1960, with the World Bank's mediation, to share the waters of the Indus river system.
Both countries tested nuclear devices in 1998 (India in May, Pakistan soon after). This intensified an arms race between them.
India has accused Pakistan of supporting cross-border terrorism and militant groups, while the two sides have also tried confidence-building measures and dialogue at times.

example.q: List three non-Kashmir disputes between India and Pakistan.
steps: Sir Creek in the Rann of Kutch.

learn.reallife: Farmers in Punjab depend on the Indus river system, which is why the 1960 water treaty matters as much to agriculture as to diplomacy.

games.title: Match the issue
pairs: Boundary in the Rann of Kutch

quiz.q: The Indus Waters Treaty between India and Pakistan was signed in:
quiz.explain: It was signed in 1960 with World Bank mediation.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with the Shimla Agreement (1972)

quiz.q: Which institution mediated the Indus Waters Treaty?
quiz.explain: The World Bank brokered the treaty.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with the Soviet-mediated Tashkent Agreement

quiz.q: Sir Creek is a dispute over:
options: A boundary line in the Rann of Kutch
An island in the Bay of Bengal
quiz.explain: Sir Creek is a strip of water in the Rann of Kutch.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with Siachen

quiz.q: The Kargil conflict between India and Pakistan took place in:
quiz.explain: It was fought in 1999, a year after the nuclear tests.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with the 1998 tests

quiz.q: In which year did both India and Pakistan conduct nuclear tests?
quiz.explain: India tested in May 1998 and Pakistan followed soon after.
quiz.mistake: Picks India's first test of 1974

quiz.q: Which has been the core issue between India and Pakistan since 1947?
quiz.explain: Kashmir has been central to most conflicts.
quiz.mistake: Picks disputes with other neighbours

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The arms race between India and Pakistan intensified after 1998. Reason (R): Both countries conducted nuclear tests in 1998.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true, and the tests explain the sharper arms race.
quiz.mistake: Does not link nuclear tests with the arms race

quiz.q: How many years separate the first India-Pakistan war (1947-48 ended in 1948) and the Kargil conflict (1999)?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts from 1947 instead of 1948

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why do India and Pakistan keep quarrelling? Is it only about Kashmir?'
teach.praise: Got it! Kashmir is the core, with wars in 1947-48, 1965, 1971 and Kargil, plus Siachen, Sir Creek, rivers and nuclear rivalry!
teach.nudge: You said Kashmir. What other disputes are there?

learn.hook: When a coup attempt shook the Maldives in 1988, Indian paratroopers arrived within hours. India's ties with its smaller neighbours mix help, friction and deep connections.
points: India-Bangladesh: differences over sharing the waters of the Ganga and Brahmaputra, illegal migration into India and border management. They also cooperate on trade, energy, disaster management and connectivity, and Bangladesh is part of India's Look East policy.

India-Nepal: a treaty allows citizens of both countries to travel and work in each other's country without visas and passports. Friction has arisen over Nepal's ties with China, trade and the Maoist movement, yet economic, scientific and cultural ties remain strong.
India-Sri Lanka: the Tamil issue and the IPKF strained ties, but relations have improved. A free trade agreement was signed, and India helped Sri Lanka after the 2004 tsunami.
India-Bhutan: a very close relationship. India supports hydroelectric projects in Bhutan, and Bhutan's king helped flush out guerrillas from north-eastern India operating from Bhutanese territory.
India-Maldives: in 1988, when mercenaries attacked the Maldives, India's air force and navy responded quickly at the Maldives' request (Operation Cactus).

example.q: Which neighbour fits each clue: (a) open border, no visa needed (b) hydroelectric partner (c) Operation Cactus (1988)?
steps: (c) Maldives: India foiled the 1988 coup attempt.

learn.reallife: Electricity from Bhutan's hydro plants lights homes in eastern India, and Nepali workers are a familiar part of many Indian cities.

games.title: True or false?
items: Citizens of India and Nepal can travel to each other's country without visas.
India refused to help the Maldives in 1988.
India's forces responded quickly at the Maldives' request.
Bhutan helped flush out guerrillas from north-east India.
Bhutan's king acted against groups operating from Bhutan.
India and Bangladesh have no disputes at all.
Water sharing, migration and border issues have caused friction.

quiz.q: Which neighbour's citizens can travel and work in India without visas and passports under a treaty?
quiz.explain: The India-Nepal treaty allows this open movement.
quiz.mistake: Assumes all neighbours have open borders

quiz.q: Operation Cactus (1988) refers to India's help to:
options: The Maldives against a coup attempt by mercenaries
quiz.explain: India sent forces at the Maldives' request.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with the IPKF in Sri Lanka

quiz.q: Which neighbour has close cooperation with India on hydroelectric projects?
quiz.explain: India supports many hydro projects in Bhutan.
quiz.mistake: Picks an island nation with no big rivers

quiz.q: A major issue between India and Bangladesh has been:
options: Sharing of Ganga and Brahmaputra waters
quiz.explain: Water sharing, migration and border issues are key topics.
quiz.mistake: Picks an India-Pakistan dispute

quiz.q: Which factor has caused friction in India-Nepal relations?
options: Nepal's ties with China and the Maoist movement
quiz.explain: Nepal's warm ties with China and Maoist activity worried India.
quiz.mistake: Picks an unrealistic option

quiz.q: India helped Sri Lanka after the 2004 tsunami. Which other step improved ties?
quiz.explain: The free trade agreement strengthened economic ties.
quiz.mistake: Assumes ties stayed hostile after the IPKF

quiz.q: Assertion (A): India-Bhutan relations are very close. Reason (R): Bhutan's king helped flush out guerrillas from north-eastern India, and India supports Bhutan's hydro projects.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; security cooperation and economic support explain the close ties.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect cooperation with closeness

quiz.q: Case: Floodwaters in the Brahmaputra affect both Assam and Bangladesh, and both countries share early warning data. This shows:
options: India and Bangladesh have cut all ties
Bangladesh is part of SAARC's military
Cooperation on disaster management alongside disputes
quiz.explain: Neighbours cooperate on shared problems even when other disputes exist.
quiz.mistake: Thinks disputes rule out cooperation

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Besides Pakistan, how does India get along with its other neighbours?'
teach.praise: Neat! Water issues with Bangladesh, an open border with Nepal, hydropower with Bhutan, help for the Maldives and better ties with Sri Lanka!
teach.nudge: Good. Which neighbour shares an open border with India, and which did India help in 1988?

learn.hook: South Asia is home to a huge share of the world's people, yet trade among its countries remains small. SAARC was meant to change that.
points: The South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) was set up in 1985 by the South Asian states to cooperate by peaceful means. Afghanistan later joined, and its secretariat is in Kathmandu.
Members signed the South Asian Free Trade Area (SAFTA) agreement in 2004, aiming to lower trade barriers across the region. It came into effect in 2006.
Some neighbours feared SAFTA would let India dominate their markets, while India's small neighbours also saw benefits from its large market.
SAARC's progress has been limited mainly by India-Pakistan tensions and political differences among members.

Outside powers matter in South Asia: China has close strategic ties with Pakistan and growing links with other neighbours, and the USA has become an important player, keeping good relations with both India and Pakistan. Comparing democracy across states and evaluating SAARC are common exercise themes.

example.q: Evaluate SAARC in two points: one achievement and one limitation.
steps: Achievement: SAFTA (2004) as a step towards regional free trade.
Limitation: progress held back by India-Pakistan tensions.
example.answer: SAFTA was achieved, but India-Pakistan tensions limit SAARC

learn.reallife: Students from all eight SAARC countries study at the South Asian University in New Delhi, set up by SAARC states, showing cooperation beyond trade.

items.text: SAFTA stands for South Asian Free ___ Area.
The country that joined SAARC later as its eighth member is ___.

games.title: Help or hindrance to SAARC?
items: Common problems like floods and poverty

quiz.q: SAARC was established in:
quiz.explain: SAARC came into being in 1985.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with ASEAN (1967) or SAFTA (2004)

quiz.q: The SAFTA agreement was signed in:
quiz.explain: SAFTA was signed in 2004 and came into effect in 2006.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the signing year with when it took effect

quiz.q: What is the main aim of SAFTA?
options: Lowering trade barriers among South Asian countries
quiz.explain: SAFTA aims at freer trade in the region.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up trade with security or currency goals

quiz.q: The main obstacle to SAARC's progress has been:
options: Absence of any trade in South Asia
quiz.explain: Rivalry between the two largest members has held SAARC back.
quiz.mistake: Overlooks the central bilateral conflict

quiz.q: Why did some smaller South Asian states fear SAFTA?
options: They feared China would leave SAARC
They thought SAFTA would ban all imports
They believed it would end their independence
They worried India would dominate their markets
quiz.explain: Smaller economies feared competition from India's large economy.
quiz.mistake: Misreads the fear as one about sovereignty only

quiz.q: Which outside power has close strategic ties with Pakistan?
quiz.explain: China's partnership with Pakistan is a key factor in South Asia.
quiz.mistake: Picks a South Asian state instead of an outside power

quiz.q: Assertion (A): SAARC has made limited progress. Reason (R): Political differences, especially between India and Pakistan, have slowed it.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; R is the main reason for slow progress.
quiz.mistake: Fails to connect tensions with slow progress

quiz.q: Assertion (A): SAARC was formed by ASEAN countries. Reason (R): SAARC aims at regional cooperation by peaceful means.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: SAARC was formed by South Asian states. R is true.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up SAARC with ASEAN

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What is SAARC, and why doesn't it work as well as the EU?'
teach.praise: Hooray! SAARC began in 1985, SAFTA came in 2004, but India-Pakistan tensions slow it down, and outside powers like China and the US matter too!
teach.nudge: Good. What trade agreement did SAARC sign, and what holds SAARC back?
